# What no general algorithm can decide

- A Turing machine models computation with finite control and an unbounded tape; it is a mathematical model, not a claim about physical memory.
- Suppose H(P,x) always decides whether P halts on x. Define D(P): loop if H(P,P) says halt; otherwise halt.
- D(D) contradicts either prediction. Therefore a universally correct halting decider cannot exist.

**Try:** Explain both cases of D(D), then say why this does not prevent deciding a particular simple loop.

# Change a heap and trace its tree

- A zero-based binary heap stores root at0; children of i are2i+1 and2i+2 when present, parent is floor((i−1)/2) for i>0.

# Choose a proof direction

- For P→Q, the converse is Q→P; the contrapositive is ¬Q→¬P and is equivalent to the original.
- Contradiction instead assumes the negation of the claim; for an implication, assume P and ¬Q, then derive impossibility.
- Claim over all integers n: if n² is even, then n is even. Every integer is even (2k) or odd (2k+1) for some integer k.

**Try:** State P and Q, converse, contrapositive and contradiction assumptions. Choose the contrapositive and prove it algebraically. Explain why that direction is useful and why numerical examples or proving the converse alone would not establish the original claim.
cases.limit: Written examples and predictions are not learner execution. External practical work needs actual reported outcome/evidence; optional practice gives no grade.
cases.title: Choose a proof direction

workedExamples.content: P: n² even; Q: n even. Converse: n even→n² even. Contrapositive: n odd→n² odd. Let n=2k+1; n²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd. Parity's two exhaustive cases make not-even equivalent to odd. This direction gives an explicit representation to expand. Contradiction starts with n² even AND n odd. The converse happens to be true but is a different implication; finitely many examples do not prove a claim over all integers.

# Construct a recognizer from two machines

- Input alphabet is {0,1}; read one symbol at a time. A DFA accepts only if its final state is accepting.
- Machine A recognizes “contains101.” States E(no useful suffix), P(suffix1), Q(suffix10), F(found). Start E; only F accepts.

| A state | on0 | on1 |
|---|---|---|
| E | E | P |
| P | Q | P |
| Q | E | F |
| F | F | F |

- Machine B tracks parity of 1s: start V(even); 0 keeps its state, 1 toggles V↔O. Only V accepts.
- A product state is (A-state,B-state); each symbol updates both components. Accept only when both components accept.

**Try:** Construct all eight product states and their two transitions, start and accepting set. Trace empty input,101,1011,10101. Explain how the construction handles an occurrence overlapping an earlier101 and why it recognizes the intersection.

cases.title: Construct a recognizer from two machines

Empty ends EV rejects.101: EV→PO→QO→FV accepts.1011 adds FO rejects.10101: EV→PO→QO→FV→FV→FO rejects (three1s); contains101 remains found despite overlap. cases.inputAndTask:
# Transform one decision problem into another

- Problem A: given a finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) and integer k with0≤k≤|V|, does G have a clique of size at least k? A clique has every pair joined.
- Problem B: on the same domain, does a graph have an independent set of size at least k? An independent set has no joined pair.
- Build complement H on the same vertices: each pair of distinct vertices is an edge in H exactly when it is not an edge in G. Keep k unchanged; never add self-loops.

**Try:** Transform G with V={a,b,c}, E={ab,bc}, first k=2 then k=3. Give H's edges and both answers, with witnesses or impossibility reasons. Explain both directions for an arbitrary subset, the empty graph with k=0, and why testing all vertex pairs takes polynomial work. State what a solver for B would let you solve.
cases.limit: Written examples and predictions are not learner execution. External practical work needs actual reported outcome/evidence; optional practice gives no grade.
cases.title: Transform one decision problem into another

workedExamples.content: H has only ac. At k=2, G has clique{a,b} (or{b,c}); the same set is independent in H. At k=3, G lacks ac and H contains ac, so both answers are no. For any subset S, every distinct pair is in E iff no such pair is in H; thus clique in G iff independent in H. Empty subset witnesses k=0 even on the empty graph. Examine n(n−1)/2 pairs, O(n²) adjacency decisions under fixed-cost pair lookup. A B solver after this transformation decides A; this construction alone proves no NP-completeness claim.

workedExamples.content: Reversing the direction of the solver claim or introducing loops breaks this reduction.
